Source: A manuscript seen and photographed by Rahul Sankrityayan in Lhasa in 1935, as reported therein. The plates subsequently went to Wogihara, who passed them on to Enomoto. The publication also contains these plates. %NB This does not appear to correspond to Tōhoku No. 3800, which is claimed to be its translation; this discrepancy was already noted by Nagao in his review. The manuscript does not contain the complete text, but only comments on Chapter 8 of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.

In fact, the closest parallel I can find is Abhayākaragupta’s *Munimatālaṃkāra* (D 217a1 ff.), which was in turn copied by Daśabalaśrīmitra’s *Saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛtaviniścaya* (D 289b2 ff.). Thus, it may well be that this is indeed the work of Jñānapāda after all! Input: Péter-Dániel Szántó [1] oṃ namaḥ sarvagurubuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ |

For one who has realized the single-moment perfect awakening consisting of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), the eighth realization is the realization of the *dharmakāya* consisting of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) in the second moment. Due to the abandonment of all afflictive and cognitive obstructions (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*) along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*) without remainder, there arise the twenty-first and twenty-second productions of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), which are of the nature of the fundamental and the subsequent [moments], known as Samantabhadra and also named Samantaprabha, characterized by absolute and supreme purity.

The stage of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhabhūmi*), which is the primary state of the fruit of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), is the eighth. "Dharma" refers to the Path; it is the eighth because it consists of the seven realizations (*abhisamaya*). It is called the "Dharma-body" because it is a body obtained through the Dharma. Through the attainment of this, the Blessed One, being beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), abides in the great fruit. In that regard, the realization of the Dharma-body is fourfold, namely: the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*), and the transformation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*) together with its activities. With reference to the essential body, he says:
The body of the Sage in its essential nature is characterized by the intrinsic nature of those untainted phenomena that have attained purity in all its aspects. (ASA 8.1)

Thus: those factors beginning with the applications of mindfulness and ending with omniscience—which are supramundane, have the *dharmadhātu* as their intrinsic nature, and are untainted (*anāsrava*) because they have abandoned the taints of desire, views, existence, and ignorance—have attained a purity in all its aspects, characterized by natural isolation, since these taints are merely adventitious; having reached that very essence, their nature is the perfectly pure *tathatā*, which is the *dharmatā*. That which has this as its characteristic is the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body), in the sense of being uncontrived. This is the "body" (*śarīra*).

And because it is the locus of all mundane and supramundane qualities, and because it pervades the universe through that [nature], such is the body of the Blessed One, the Sage, the Perfectly Awakened One, which is attained by means of the supramundane path. Conventionally, it is not made an object, it is not created, and it is not produced. It is realized through the practice of all phenomena. And that is to be personally realized by the Perfectly Awakened One alone, and not by anyone else. Having thus established the *svābhāvikakāya*, he speaks of the *dharmakāya* as follows:
The factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the liberations, and the successive meditative attainments...
The ninefold meditative attainment, the tenfold totalities,
the eight types of bases of mastery according to their divisions,
the absence of conflict, the knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges.
Then there are the four purities in all their aspects, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the state of having nothing to guard,
the threefold application of mindfulness, and the threefold quality of being free from forgetfulness.
The complete eradication of latent predispositions, great compassion for beings,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Sage that are traditionally taught,
and the knowledge of all aspects— this is designated as the Dharma-body.

Thus: "The factors conducive to enlightenment" refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). There are seven groups, namely: 1) the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), 2) the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), 3) the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), 4) the faculties (*indriya*), 5) the powers (*bala*), 6) the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and 7) the eightfold path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Among these, there are four foundations of mindfulness, namely: 1) the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), 2) the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), 3) the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), and 4) the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): namely, 1) the desire to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising; 2) the desire to abandon arisen unwholesome states; 3) the desire to produce unarisen wholesome states; 4) the desire for the increase of arisen wholesome states. The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): namely, 1) the base of psychic power consisting of desire; 2) the base of psychic power consisting of energy; 3) the base of psychic power consisting of mind; 4) the base of psychic power consisting of investigation.

The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*). Namely: 1) the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), 2) the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), 3) the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), 4) the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and 5) the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

The five powers (*pañca balāni*). Namely: 1) the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), 2) the power of energy (*vīryabala*), 3) the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), 4) the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), and 5) the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
These are mundane (*laukika*).

[5] The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). They are as follows: 1) the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*); 2) the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*); 3) the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*); 4) the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*); 5) the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*prasrabdhisambodhyaṅga*); 6) the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*); and 7) the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*). The eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*). They are as follows: 1) right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); 2) right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*); 3) right speech (*samyagvāk*); 4) right action (*samyakkarmānta*); 5) right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); 6) right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); 7) right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*); and 8) right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
The immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are four: (1) loving-kindness (*maitrī*), (2) compassion (*karuṇā*), (3) sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and (4) equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The liberations (*vimokṣa*) are eight, as follows: (1) possessing form, one perceives forms—this is the first liberation; (2) being internally formless, one perceives external forms—this is the second; (3) being resolved upon the beautiful (*śubha*)—this is the third; (4) the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is the fourth; (5) the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is the fifth; (6) the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is the sixth; (7) the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the seventh.

The eighth is the liberation of the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpattivimokṣa). [6] There are nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ), namely: the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (ārūpyas), and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. [9] There are ten totalities (daśa kṛtsnāni), namely: the earth-totality (pṛthivīkṛtsna) 1; the water-totality (āpkṛtsna) 2; the fire-totality (tejaḥkṛtsna) 3; the air-totality (vāyukṛtsna) 4; the blue-totality (nīlakṛtsna) 5; the yellow-totality (pītakṛtsna) 6; the red-totality (lohitakṛtsna) 7; the white-totality (avadātakṛtsna) 8; the space-infinity-totality (ākāśānantyāyatanakṛtsna) 9; and the consciousness-infinity-totality (vijñānānantyāyatanakṛtsna) 10.

There are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). They are as follows: 1. One who perceives forms internally sees forms externally that are limited; having mastered them, one knows and sees them—this is the first base of mastery. 2. One who perceives forms internally sees forms externally that are vast; having mastered them, one knows and sees them, and likewise becomes one who possesses that perception—this is the second.

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited; having mastered them, one knows and sees them—this is the third [base of mastery]. Likewise, "extensive" is the fourth. Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, and so forth as before—this is the fifth. Likewise, "yellow" is the sixth. Likewise, "red" is the seventh. Likewise, "white" is the eighth.

[7] *Raṇa* refers to strife, disputes, quarrels, and so forth; however, in this context, the affliction (*kleśa*) that is the cause of strife is itself termed *raṇa*. It is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that one enters by the power of a previous vow, thinking, "May no strife arise among these beings with me as its object. Because of this, once one has emerged from that state and entered a village or similar place, no strife arises among the sentient beings there by taking him as their object; this is *sāraṇā*.

The six superknowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) are as follows: 1) the superknowledge of supernormal powers (*ṛddhy-abhijñā*); 2) the superknowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*); 3) the superknowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*); 4) the superknowledge of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*); 5) the superknowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*); and 6) the superknowledge of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna-abhijñā*). The four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisamvidaḥ*) are as follows: 1) the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisamvit*); 2) the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisamvit*); 3) the analytical knowledge of etymological expression (*niruktipratisamvit*); and 4) the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisamvit*).

There are four purifications, namely: (1) purification of the basis (*āśrayapariśuddhi*), (2) purification of the object (*ālambanapariśuddhi*), (3) purification of the mind (*cittapariśuddhi*), and (4) purification of knowledge (*jñānapariśuddhi*). Among these, (1) purification of the basis is the absolute cessation of all forms of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of all afflictions along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*) from the basis, as well as mastery in every respect over the taking up, remaining, and casting off of one’s own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) according to one’s will. (2) Purification of the object is mastery in every respect over the manifestation, transformation, and enumeration of all objects.
As before, there is the departure of all mental dysfunctions, mastery over the knowledge of all that is to be known, and the complete purification of knowledge in all its aspects.

There are ten masteries (*vaśitā*). They are as follows: 1. Mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*): because one establishes or relinquishes the lifespan according to one’s wish. 2. Mastery over mind (*citta-vaśitā*): because one exercises mastery over meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and so forth, according to one’s wish, through the empowerment of a lifespan-measure for inexpressible eons, and by emerging from those attainments at will. 3. Mastery over requisites (*pariṣkāra-vaśitā*): because one displays the empowerment of all world-systems adorned with various arrays and ornaments, and because one provides the necessary conditions and supports according to one’s wish.

[9] Mastery over action (*karmavaśitā*) results from the accomplishment of bodily and vocal actions according to one's wish, and from the manifestation of the empowerment of the maturation of karma at the appropriate time. Mastery over rebirth (*upapattivaśitā*) results from taking birth at will in all places of rebirth. Mastery over supernatural power (*ṛddhivaśitā*) consists of the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*)—such as the display of miraculous transformations in all Buddha-fields—as one wishes. Mastery over aspiration (*praṇidhānavaśitā*) results from the fulfillment of all vows. Mastery over resolve (*adhimuktivaśitā*) is such that whatever one resolves upon occurs exactly in that way.

Mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*) is the ability to know whatever one wishes to know, such as the manifestation of all world-systems filled with Buddhas, or the vision of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a Buddha, the primary and secondary marks, and the realization of perfect awakening. Mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*) is skillfulness in the systematic arrangements of the Sūtras and Abhidharma. (10)

There are three things that need no protection. They are as follows: The Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is completely pure; there is no impurity of bodily conduct that he would consider needing to conceal so that others might not know of it—this is the first thing that needs no protection. Likewise, his verbal action is the second. His mental action is the third.

[10] There are three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). They are as follows: When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, some listen with a desire to hear, lend an ear, apply their minds to understanding, and practice in accordance with the Dharma; yet because of this, the Tathāgata feels no delight, no joy, and no elation of mind. Others do not listen, do not lend an ear, and so forth.

Because of that, the Tathāgata has no resentment, no impatience, no lack of affection, and no mental displeasure. Some listen respectfully while others do not; because of this, there is no duality in the Tathāgata—neither delight nor resentment. He dwells everywhere in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.

The quality of non-forgetfulness consists in not missing the proper time for acting for the benefit of sentient beings. The latent predisposition of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) is that activity which, even in one who has abandoned the afflictions, appears as if they had not abandoned them; it is like the subtle fragrance remaining in jars, clothes, and so forth, even after the sesame flowers or other sources have been removed. Among these, the predisposition of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*) is that which acts as an obstruction to the discernment of the objects of knowledge. The predispositions of attachment and the rest are also the cause of specific modes of physical and vocal activity, such as the jumping movements of a monk who was previously a monkey.

And regarding the speech [of the Buddha] that formerly addressed a *vṛṣalī* as a *brāhmaṇī*: all such [instances] have likewise come to an end for the Tathāgata; thus, the Blessed One is said to have eradicated the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions. Therefore, this Blessed One possesses the total eradication of latent predispositions. When the Blessed One, out of a desire for welfare, surveys the world six times every day and night in such forms as "Who is declining? Who is prospering? and so forth, that desire for welfare is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The knowledge of the ultimate limit of the distinctions between the essential natures and specific characteristics of all phenomena is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The ten powers are as follows: 1) the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; 2) the power of knowing the ripening of karma; 3) the power of knowing the various elements; 4) the power of knowing the various inclinations; 5) the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; 6) the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere; 7) the power of knowing the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; 8) the power of knowing the recollection of former abodes; 9) the power of knowing death and rebirth.

The tenth is the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*). Their characteristics are found in the Sūtra: "Regarding what is possible and impossible, [the Buddha] knows the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible; and the cause is the possible. For example: he understands what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. In this regard, it is possible that misconduct has an undesirable ripening, whereas an desirable ripening is impossible. It is possible that good conduct has a desirable ripening, whereas an undesirable ripening is impossible. It is possible that stinginess leads to poverty, whereas great wealth is impossible.

Through generosity, great wealth is possible; poverty is impossible. It is impossible for one who has committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*)—characterized by killing one's mother, father, or an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or maliciously drawing blood from a Tathāgata—to have their mind remain stable. Likewise, it is impossible for the mind to remain stable in one who violates his mother who is an Arhatī, kills a Bodhisattva fixed in the [path of] certainty, kills a Śaikṣa, steals the property of the Saṅgha used for its gateway, or destroys a stūpa—these being the five near-immediate transgressions.

For one established in regret, mental pliancy is impossible. For a woman, to attain the state of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or Brahmā in that very same body is impossible. Conversely, everything is possible. He knows such possibilities and impossibilities through pure, unattached, and unimpeded knowledge. In this context, "pure" means non-erroneous according to reality; by the repetition "whatever is real," it signifies being unattached.

In whatever manner it is real, because of his knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*), he is unimpeded. That very knowledge is a power (*bala*) because it is absolutely invincible by others. Karma consists of the meritorious (*puṇya*), the non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and the imperturbable (*āniñjya*). Among these, that which is associated with the fourth dhyāna and that which is associated with the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), when wholesome, is established as meritorious. Ripening (*vipāka*) refers to pleasure, pain, and so forth. The "various elements" (*nānādhātu*) refers to the underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*) for producing meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable [karma]. "Various inclinations" (*nānādhimukti*) refers to various tastes; for example:

Even for one established in passion, there is a preference for hatred; even for one established in hatred, there is a preference for passion; for one whose practice is inferior, there is a preference for sublime practice; for one whose practice is sublime, there is a preference for inferior practice—and so forth.

The faculties (*indriya*) are faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Their relative degree—whether superior or inferior—is their state of being weak, middling, or intense. For example: "This one has weak faculties; this one has middling faculties," and so forth. [14] The path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī pratipat*): here, one knows the destiny of beings within the realm of sentient beings as being either fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata*) or unfixed (*aniyata*). Furthermore, one knows and teaches the appropriate paths for those who are fixed and those who are unfixed.

Knowing them to be fixed in falsehood, equanimity alone is appropriate toward them; thus, for that duration, he remains equanimous. He understands that "this is the path that serves as the antidote to attachment" and "this is the path that serves as the antidote to aversion. Furthermore, he knows the defilement, purification, and emergence of the four dhyānas, the eight liberations, the concentrations with and without applied and sustained thought, and the four formless attainments—the serial attainments of meditative dwelling. In this context, "defilement" refers to [the mind] being tainted by relishing and so forth.

Purification is by means of non-apprehension and so forth. Emergence is either by the lion’s yawn or by the leaping-over [meditative absorption]. Previous abodes refers to previous births; recollection of them is memory. Passing away and rebirth refers to the death and birth of sentient beings.
This was stated in the *Āryadharaṇīśvararājasūtra*.

[15] In this regard, this is the divine eye of the Tathāgata, by which he sees, throughout the worlds in the ten directions as far as the limits of the realm of space, whatever manifestations of fields there may be—whether they are being consumed by fire, undergoing dissolution, or undergoing evolution; and whatever manifestations of sentient beings there may be, all of them passing away and being reborn; and even those sentient beings who have gone beyond the range of light, so that they too come within the range of the Tathāgata’s divine eye.

Even though it is said that the sense faculties have the nature of *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption), because the sense faculty—which has the nature of ignorance—is abandoned in the state of Buddhahood, all of the Blessed One’s consciousness is held to have all objects as its domain through the cognition of the sense faculties, which—like the mental cognition (*manovijñāna*)—delimits the object of thought.
And this is stated in the *Ārya-śraddhābalādhāna-sūtra*:

In this way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata sees even with his *uṣṇīṣa*, and he sees even with his *ūrṇā*. He sees even with each individual mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, simultaneously, he sees throughout the entire expansion of world-systems in the ten directions. Nevertheless, because sensory cognition is established according to its prior continuity, it is called "divine eye," "divine ear," and so forth. || [16] || Furthermore, "the destruction of the outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*) for sentient beings refers to both the outflows—which are all the afflictions (*kleśa*)—and the path by which their destruction occurs.

One who is utterly fearless like a lion and speaks what is appropriate is called "confident" (*viśārada*). His state or activity is "confidence" (*vaiśāradya*), which is fourfold. Namely: 1) confidence regarding perfect enlightenment; 2) confidence regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); 3) confidence regarding obstacles; and 4) confidence regarding the factors leading to liberation (*nairyāṇika-dharma*).

In this context, perfect enlightenment is the Tathāgata’s perfection of knowledge; the destruction of the outflows is his perfection of abandonment. Both of these constitute his own welfare (*svārtha*). Obstructive factors are those that hinder deliverance; conducive factors are those that lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa. Both of these constitute the welfare of others (*parārtha*), because he proclaims them to others. Fearlessness regarding these [four points] is [the Buddha's confidence]. ||o||

[17] The twelvefold teaching of the Tathāgatas is *dharma*. Its entire subject matter is *artha*. The various etymological explanations (*nirvacana*) of those very designators of the *dharma*—namely, the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*)—are *nirukti*. Alternatively, all causal phenomena (*hetudharma*) are *dharma*, and all resultant phenomena (*phaladharma*) are *artha*. All languages of sentient beings included within the six realms of existence are *nirukti*. The analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*) pertain to these *dharma*, *artha*, and *nirukti*.

In their respective order, there are the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisamvit*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisamvit*), and the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisamvit*). The manifestation of the analytical knowledges of phenomena and so forth for the purpose of elucidating the gates of phenomena and so on is *pratibhāna* (eloquence). Since eloquence arises from that [analytical knowledge], it is called the "analytical knowledge of eloquence" (*pratibhānapratisamvit*); thus, within the analytical knowledge of eloquence, all four analytical knowledges are included. ||o||

Because they proceed in a manner that is unrivaled, these are the qualities unique to the Buddhas alone; thus, there are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). They are as follows: [18] There is no stumbling for the Tathāgata. (1) Just as Arhats who wander through villages and other places for alms may encounter harm from fierce elephants, horses, cattle, dogs, thorns, reptiles, and the like, or face fear from thieves, tigers, and so forth—such things do not exist for the Tathāgata in any way whatsoever. And it is said in the *Dharaṇīśvararāja-sūtra*:

For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess unerring physical actions and a graceful deportment. In the four modes of conduct—whether entering or departing from villages and cities—their feet touch the earth with their soles, and upon that great earth, thousand-spoked wheels appear; furthermore, lotuses of delightful fragrance spring forth.

Wherever the Tathāgata sets foot, those beings who have been born into the animal realm who are touched by the Tathāgata’s fearlessness shall for seven nights be endowed with supreme happiness, and upon passing away, they will be reborn among the gods. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s robe falls upon his body at a distance of four finger-breadths; even by the Bhairambha winds it cannot be moved.

[19] Furthermore, the radiance of the Tathāgata’s body brings happiness to sentient beings as far down as the Avīci hell; therefore, it is said that there is no physical lapse for the Tathāgata, because he always acts with full awareness (1).

There is no shouting from the Tathāgata. For example, an Arhat who has gone onto a path leading through a forest might raise his voice loudly, or break into loud laughter due to the force of residual impressions (*vāsanā*); but such is not the case for the Tathāgata, because he is eternally in a state of meditative concentration (2).

The Tathāgata has no loss of mindfulness. This is because an Arhat, when not attending to something, acts with lost mindfulness, fails to perform his duty, and lets the proper time pass; the Buddha is not like this, owing to his great compassion (mahākāruṇikatva). (3) The Tathāgata has no state of non-concentrated mind. This is because an Arhat is concentrated only when he has entered meditative absorption (samāpanna), and at other times he is not; the Buddha is not like this, owing to his being eternally concentrated. (4)

The Tathāgata has no perception of diversity. Just as an Arhat exclusively perceives material substrates (*upadhi*) as disagreeable and perceives Nirvāṇa as peaceful, the Buddha is not like that; because of the selflessness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-nairātmyatā*), he is non-conceptual with respect to both. (5) The Tathāgata has no equanimity resulting from lack of deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyāyopekṣā*). Just as an Arhat neglects the welfare of sentient beings through lack of deliberation, the Buddha is not like that; for he remains impartial precisely by not deliberating on time and other such factors, and not otherwise. (6)

The Tathāgata has no decline in his zeal (*chanda*). In this regard, his zeal consists of loving-kindness and compassion, the teaching of the Dharma, the training and maturing of sentient beings, seclusion, and the inciting of others toward awakening. This [zeal] does not belong to a disciple (*śrāvaka*). The Tathāgata has no decline in his vigor (*vīrya*). In this regard, his vigor consists of the vigor of those to be trained and the vigor of instruction for those who listen to the Dharma. For instance, if the Tathāgata were to find such a listener of the Dharma who would not grow weary even after hearing for an eon, the Tathāgata would not rise from that state even after an eon.

While teaching the Dharma, the Tathāgata—due to his lack of need for food, the continuity of his being, and his regard for sentient beings—may traverse even as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, wherever there might be even a single sentient being who is to be disciplined by a Buddha.
(8) There is no loss of mindfulness in the Tathāgata. For it is thus: the Tathāgata does not teach the Dharma to sentient beings after having to deliberate or reflect. (9)

There is no decline of the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That is to say: concentration is the equality of all phenomena, their lack of inequality, their being just as they are. That which is equal is the equality; that which is the equality is the concentration. That which is the concentration is the Tathāgata. Because he is not dependent even upon the triple world, he neither diminishes nor declines. Therefore, it is said: "There is no decline of the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration. 10.

The Tathāgata has no decline in wisdom. That is to say: wisdom as the equality of all phenomena; knowledge that is not led by others; the illumination of the Dharma for other sentient beings; the knowledge of the distinctions of skill in the inexhaustible analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*); the knowledge of teaching through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for hundreds of thousands of eons by means of entering a single word; and the knowledge of teaching through the definitive establishment of the cutting off of doubt regarding the explanation of the meaning as it has been taught.

[22] Knowledge of the eighty-four thousand types of mental conduct of sentient beings, and the manifestation of the Dharma according to what is appropriate through the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma—this is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of infinite, inexhaustible, and immeasurable exposition. 11.

There is no falling away from liberation for the Tathāgata. For example: the liberation of the Tathāgata is free from all grasping; it was unbound from the past, does not transition to the future, and is not sustained in the present. The mind is luminous by nature, and knowledge is likewise. Therefore, it is said that he has perfectly awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment through wisdom conjoined with a single moment. 12.

All bodily action of the Tathāgata is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge. For example, whatever bodily action the Tathāgata possesses, by it he disciplines sentient beings even by his mere appearance, whether he is speaking, silent, eating, or even by his deportment and his physical marks; such is the detailed account. All vocal action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge. For example, the Tathāgata is a teacher of the Dharma that is free from bondage, and that speech of the Tathāgata is endowed with sixty aspects.

All mental action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge. That is to say: that Tathāgata-knowledge conforms to the minds of all sentient beings, is born from all phenomena, transcends all objects of perception dependent on others for what is to be accomplished, is realized through dependent origination, extends throughout the immeasurable realms of existence and destinies of the three worlds, transcends all paths of Māra, and is non-different from the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). 15. (Note: The manuscript reads *°ālaṃbaṇa* [object], while the edition opts for *°āraṃbaṇa* [dependence].)

The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision regarding the past proceeds unhindered and unimpeded. As many Buddha-fields as there are, as many grasses, shrubs, and so forth within them, as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are, and as many teachings of the Dharma for himself and others—[the Tathāgata] knows all of that through the application of calculation; and he knows it by means of direct knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), not by means of inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

[24] In the future time, his knowledge and vision proceed unhindered and unimpeded. For example: he knows by calculation in detail all that will arise—whatever fields, whatever abodes of sentient beings, and whatever thought will arise immediately after whichever thought. This is the full explanation. 17.

In the present time, his unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision proceed. For example, he knows those Buddha-fields that exist in the ten directions; he knows all phenomena, all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, up to and including all the elements such as earth, by means of dividing them into atoms and down to their placement upon the tip of a hair; and he knows the realm of sentient beings born in the destinies such as the hells, and so forth, in detail.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of a knowledge that follows after duality for the sake of entering non-duality.

(18) [25] Among these, the first is through the purification of bodily action; the second is through the purification of vocal action; the other four are through the purification of mental action. Beyond those, there are six based on the Tathāgata’s faculties together with their fruits, because of the non-existence of what has not been attained and the non-existence of the loss of what has been attained. In this context, the basis is aspiration (*chanda*), the fruit is liberation, and the faculties are vigor and the others.

Next, there are three others: the states of body, speech, and mental action being presided over by gnosis (*jñānādhiṣṭhitatva*), by virtue of being caused by gnosis and accompanying gnosis. Next, there are three others: the unattached and unimpeded gnoses regarding the three times. These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). Furthermore, "omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is explicitly mentioned, while "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*) and so forth were also previously stated. Some maintain that all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and the rest, which have been transformed through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), consist of non-conceptual gnosis and are designated as the *dharmakāya*. Others, however, [hold a different view].
The nature of those untainted phenomena that have attained purity in every aspect is the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the Sage, characterized by their intrinsic nature. (ASA 8.1)

Thus, having accepted that the supramundane, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena exist according to the literal sense, they explain that the *svābhāvikakāya* (essential body) is characterized by the nature of those phenomena, which is their non-arising (*anutpādatā*). Having explained that this very *dharmatākāya* (body of reality) is designated as the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) through the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), they raise the question: "What, then, are those untainted phenomena whose characteristic nature constitutes the *dharmakāya*? Anticipating this doubt, they introduce the verse beginning with "the factors conducive to awakening" (*bodhipakṣa*), and so forth.

Others ask: "How are the non-dual mind and mental factors—which, through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) by way of generating the appearance of distinguished objects according to the conventional reality of yogins, have undergone transformation and perform purposeful actions such as teaching the Dharma—necessarily to be accepted and included? This is stated by some in the explanation of the four bodies:

"The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), together with the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*), and likewise the other, the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*), along with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and its activity—thus it is proclaimed in four ways. (AS 1.17)

[27] Thus, because the term *dharmakāya* is not recited in the verse immediately after the word *svābhāvika*, there are only three bodies (*kāyatraya*). Others maintain that, due to the force of the purpose already indicated and for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse, this was stated specifically to connect gnosis (*jñāna*) with its activity (*kāritra*); therefore, there is no contradiction, and the fourfold body (*kāyacatuṣṭaya*) mentioned in other sections remains valid.
To demonstrate the distinction between the Buddha’s concentration of non-affliction (*araṇāsamādhi*) and that of the Śrāvakas and others, he states an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*):
"By the Śrāvaka’s vision of non-affliction, human afflictions are avoided."
In order to sever the stream of those afflictions, the Victors are without conflict even in villages and other such places.

Thus: when a *śrāvaka* perceives the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), he destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*) of human beings in villages and other places for as long as he is seen, due to the power of such a vow. However, the distinction is that for a *Tathāgata*, it completely cuts off the very continuity of the afflictions of other sentient beings as well. For all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are "conflicts" (*raṇa*); because they are absent, this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is "without conflict" (*araṇā*).
[28] In order to state the distinction between the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) of the *Tathāgata* and that of the *śrāvakas* and others, he states an intermediate verse:
Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever-present, the Buddha’s knowledge resulting from his vow is held to be that which dispels all questions. (ASA 8.8)

Thus: when one has entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) after making a formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*) such as "May I know this," the knowledge that arises regarding worldly events and so forth is the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) for the Śrāvakas. For the Tathāgatas, however, the knowledge resulting from resolve is effortless because it is non-conceptual; it is unattached because it is independent; it is unimpeded because it is unobstructed everywhere; and it is ever-present because it abides in a mind that is perpetually in a state of meditative equipoise. It resolves all questions. [29] When the cause has reached maturity, for whomever and whenever it may be—
"Benefit must be performed for that [being] for whom it is intended; such is the renown of him [the Buddha].

(ASA 8.9). Thus, when the cause—consisting of the cultivation of the focal object of the Buddhas and others through association with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth—and the seeds of previously planted roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) have reached maturity, at whatever time and for whichever sentient being the teaching of the Dharma and so forth would be beneficial for their future welfare, at that time the Blessed One, through the fulfillment of his previous vows, performs purposeful action in accordance with the appearance of that [being].

The sense is that although [the Tathāgata] is always present like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), he does not appear as one who bestows results due to a deficiency in the causes produced by the transgressions of one's own karma.
To explain how this is so, he provides an illustration with an intermediate verse (*antaraśloka*).
[30] "For even when the rain-god pours down, that which is not a seed does not sprout;
likewise, even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the potential does not enjoy what is auspicious.

(ASA 8.10) Just as when the king of gods sends rain, seeds such as sesame that have become non-seeds due to putrefaction and the like do not emerge, so too, even upon the appearance of Buddhas—who are capable of fulfilling every desire—one who lacks the potential does not obtain what is auspicious, such as hearing the True Dharma and so forth.
"Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because of its inexhaustibility, he is also called eternal.

(ASA 8.11) According to the reasoning thus stated, because the Blessed One performs purposeful action through the medium of appearing everywhere—due to the vastness [of that activity]—and because he remains in continuity throughout the duration of *saṃsāra* without exhaustion, he is respectively designated as "all-pervading" and "eternal. ||o||

[31] Having thus described the second body, he speaks of the third, the *sāmbhogika-kāya*, which is radiant with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*vyañjana*), and whose intrinsic nature is the form-body (*rūpakāya*): This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary signs, is considered the *sāmbhogika-kāya* because of its enjoyment of the Mahāyāna. (ASA 8.12)

Thus, because he enjoys the joy and bliss of partaking in the supreme, irreproachable Mahāyāna Dharma together with the great Bodhisattvas who have entered the ten stages, this third body of the Blessed Buddha—the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*)—should be understood as having the nature of the form body (*rūpakāya*), its limbs adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

The activity of establishing [beings] in the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), by teaching that the perfections and other qualities of the bodhisattvas, their threefold limit (*koṭi-traya*), and their fruit are all empty of intrinsic nature, so that by cultivating that [emptiness], they eventually attain unsurpassed enlightenment;

8. The activity of establishing [beings] in the non-dual dharma, by teaching that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, that those very phenomena are themselves the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and that [phenomena and emptiness] are non-dual.

In regard to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the Blessed One has not apprehended any phenomenon whatsoever from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); however, having fully awakened to conventional phenomena, he taught them—the aggregates, elements, and so forth; the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth; and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and so forth. This is the activity of establishing conventional knowledge (9).

If, while practicing among all phenomena such as the perfections, one does not apprehend their three limits (*koṭitraya*) nor their fruit, then one is able to attain perfect enlightenment; this is the activity of establishing non-apprehension (10).

Even though a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive sentient beings from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he nevertheless perceives them conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) as being afflicted by their attachment to things. He brings them to maturity within the three vehicles for the sake of abandoning that [attachment]; this is the activity of establishing the maturation of sentient beings (11).

Practicing each of the perfections and so forth, he trains all sentient beings in all pure qualities (*śukladharma*) and in the emptiness of all phenomena; this is the activity of establishing [sentient beings] on the path of the bodhisattva (12).

He examines in this way: "All phenomena are empty," yet he does not become attached even to emptiness itself. He thinks, "One should practice giving and the other perfections, yet one should not conceive of them or their fruits. This is the activity of establishing the abandonment of all attachments (13).

"Awakening itself is the path, and the path itself is awakening. Yet, in this way, the bodhisattva would not be a Buddha. For when he, having fulfilled all the qualities of a Buddha, attains perfect awakening, only then is he a Tathāgata. This is the activity of establishing the attainment of awakening (14).

Having warded off the dysfunctions of all conceptualizations regarding the aggregates, elements, and so forth, he establishes both himself and others in all virtues such as the perfections (*pāramitā*). He dedicates that virtue toward the perfect enlightenment of himself and others, as well as the purification of his own Buddha-field, and makes aspirational prayers; this is the activity of establishing the purification of the Buddha-field (15).

From the very first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*), the bodhisattva becomes fixed in perfect enlightenment; and for one who is thus fixed, there is no rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*); this is the activity of establishing certainty in perfect enlightenment (16).

Abiding in the perfection of wisdom, he works for the benefit of sentient beings in the incalculable world-systems of the ten directions, yet he is not defiled; established in emptiness, he becomes established in all pure dharmas. Because there is no otherness between emptiness and all dharmas, this is the activity of establishing immeasurable sentient beings in their welfare. 17.

He investigates in this way: "The world-systems in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and the Tathāgatas who reside within them—all these are empty by their very nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). If, however, there were no emptiness for anything, that [emptiness] would be merely partial. Therefore, abiding in the *prajñāpāramitā*—realizing that 'all phenomena are empty of all phenomena'—he brings forth the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). This is the activity of establishing the approach to the Buddhas of the ten directions and so forth. 18. % tu] em., nu ed.

[53] What are the factors of enlightenment for a bodhisattva? They are the six perfections up to the unique qualities of a Buddha; this is the activity of establishing the factors of enlightenment (19). Although all phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics from the perspective of ultimate truth, nevertheless, from the perspective of conventional truth, there is action and there is its fruit. Yet sentient beings do not know that phenomena are empty of intrinsic characteristics. Not knowing this, they conceptualize persons and phenomena and thereby perform karmic formations. Through such misconduct, they fall into the three lower realms; through good conduct, they are reborn among gods and humans.

Furthermore, some, having fully understood the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and having abandoned both happy and miserable destinies, attain *nirvāṇa*. Bodhisattvas, however, while fulfilling the wholesome dharmas such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the two kinds of selflessness, gradually reach the tenth stage; then, through wisdom conjoined with a single moment, they perfectly awaken to all phenomena and become Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. This is the twenty-first activity: the establishment of the non-disappearance of the connection between action and its fruit.

[54] A bodhisattva does not attain nirvāṇa through the cognitions of the truths; rather, by means of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the four truths, he fully understands suffering, abandons its origin, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path. This is the activity of establishing the four truths (21). The four perversions—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, non-self as self, and what belongs to the self as "mine"—are the opposites of the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*). Clinging to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa*) is the opposite of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). This is the activity of establishing the abandonment of perversion (22).

Through perversion (*viparyāsa*), sentient beings perform karmic formations; consequently, they become defiled by way of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is the activity of establishing the knowledge that perversion is devoid of intrinsic substance (23). That which is the equality of all phenomena—the suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—is called "nirvāṇa"; this is the activity of establishing purification (24).

[55] The Bodhisattva practices the accumulations (*sambhāra*) for the sake of abandoning the perversions of all sentient beings, and having attained full awakening, liberates those beings; this is the activity of establishing the accumulation of purification (25).

For equality is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and there is no diversity within the true nature of phenomena. It is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; and that which is conditioned or unconditioned—both of these are neither conjoined nor disjoined, and are without characteristics. This is the activity of establishing knowledge through the non-differentiation of the conditioned and the unconditioned (26). All phenomena are empty by their own nature; therefore, it was established by the Tathāgatas that whatever is emptiness of intrinsic nature, which is the exhaustion of the grasping after existence and non-existence, that is Nirvāṇa. This is the activity of establishing [beings] in Nirvāṇa (27).

Activity (*kāritra*) is conduct (*ācāra*); its pervasiveness consists in its being uninterrupted for as long as space endures, manifesting in all forms toward all sentient beings dwelling in the world-systems of the ten directions, according to their respective capacities. [56] However, the establishment of activity according to the view of the master Haribhadra is as follows:
(1) the activity of pacifying rebirth, characterized by non-attachment and non-abiding in either auspicious or inauspicious states of existence; 1.
2. The activity of establishing [beings] in the four means of attraction, beginning with generosity.

3. The activity of establishing [beings] in the realization of affliction and purification, by means of awakening through knowledge consisting of hearing and so forth, via the door of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, namely, the adverse factors and their remedies.
4. The activity of establishing [beings] in the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, which is the altruistic aim characterized by loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].

5. The activity of establishing [beings] in the practice of the six perfections; 6. The activity of establishing [beings] in the path of the Buddha, which consists of the ten paths of wholesome action;
7. The activity of establishing [beings] in the practice of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

8. By means of the empowerment of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), on the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the activity of establishing [beings] everywhere in the exhaustion of duality, characterized by the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*.

9. On the second stage and those following, which serve as the causes for the fulfillment of the accumulations (*sambhāra*), there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the conventional knowledge of all phenomena, such as the perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth.

[57] 10. By means of the empowerment of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), on the sixth stage, there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the non-apprehension of all phenomena, characterized by non-attachment to the cultivation of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
On the seventh [ground], by the power of the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā), there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the ripening of sentient beings (11).

On the eighth [ground], by the power of the perfection of strength (bala-pāramitā), there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the bodhisattva path that is not shared with the śrāvakas and others (12).
On that very same ground, there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the abandonment of attachment to cultivation (bhāvanābhiniveśa) (13).
14. On the ninth [ground], through the power of the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*), there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the attainment of enlightenment.

15. On the tenth ground, through the power of the perfection of gnosis (*jñānapāramitā*), there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the purification of various Buddha-fields. 16. On that very same ground, there is the activity of establishing [beings] in the determination of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) for those who are bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

[58] 17. The activity of establishing [beings] for the sake of sentient beings in the world-systems of the ten directions; 18. The activity of establishing [them] in qualities such as approaching the Buddhas in all world-systems; 19. The activity of establishing [them] in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), which have the nature of the path of distinction and are characterized by the dharmas that bring about all aspects of awakening.
20. The activity of establishing [beings] in the non-perishing of the connection between action and its fruit;
21. The activity of establishing [beings] in the realization of all phenomena as they truly are;
22. The activity of establishing [beings] in the abandonment of all errors.

23. The activity of establishing [beings] in the knowledge that abandons misconceptions regarding the absence of real entities; 24. The activity of establishing [beings] in the purification of a bodhisattva, which has the characteristic of being naturally pure;
25. The activity of establishing [beings] in the accumulations, which are the cause of purification free from all stains.

26. The activity of establishing [beings] in the thorough knowledge of the non-distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned by way of the intrinsic nature of emptiness; 27. The activity of establishing [beings] in nirvāṇa on the stage of the Tathāgatas.
Thus is the determination of the activities according to the intention of the master Haribhadra. ||o||
[59] Having thus explained by way of a summary of eight topics for the sake of favoring sentient beings who delight in detail, he speaks again another explanation:
"Characteristics, their application, their excellence, their sequence, their culmination, and their maturation—this is another sixfold summary of the topics. (ASA 9.1)

Thus: first, the definition [of the path] is by virtue of its being the basis for characterizing the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Next, the "application to the three types of omniscience" (*trisarvajñatā-prayoga*) is the clear realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), because by means of this one applies oneself to the cultivation of the three types of omniscience for the sake of mastery (*vaśitā*). Then, through extreme practice, there is the attainment of excellence; thus, the "culminating clear realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*) is the stage of excellence regarding the three types of omniscience.

Then, from the ascertainment of the realized reality, there is the refinement of the meaning through its analysis and synthesis; this is the sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) situated in the order of the three types of omniscience (*trisarvajñatā*). Then, because there is no further progress toward distinction, there is the perfect awakening in a single moment (*samyagekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), which is the state of culmination regarding the three types of omniscience. Following that, its fruit is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) together with its activity (*sakāritra*), which is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three types of omniscience; thus, there is another summary of the subject matter in six aspects.

[60] The commentary on "of every mother" is to be explained exactly as before. Having thus provided an explanation by way of a compendium of six topics for the sake of benefiting sentient beings who delight in the intermediate [length], he now states another explanation for the sake of benefiting sentient beings who delight in the concise:
The object, the triad, the cause, the fourfold application, The fruit which is the dharma-body, and activity— This is another compendium of the meaning in three parts.

Thus: first, the objective (*viṣaya*) consists of the three types of omniscience, beginning with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because they constitute the domain of engagement. Following that, the fourfold application of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya-prayoga*), beginning with the realization of all aspects (*sarvākārābhisambodha*), constitutes the cause (*hetu*), answering the question of how that cause is applied. Subsequently, the result (*phala*) of that cause which possesses such application is the *dharmakāya* together with its activity; thus, another summary of the three topics has been explained in the same manner for the threefold *Jinajananī*.
